chunks: "Sure, give me a number. Let me say how I'd approach it in general, and then do an example. Every base is positional: each digit is multiplied by a power of the base.
To go to decimal I just add digit times power. For example hex 0xAF is 10 times 16 plus 15, which is 175.
To go from decimal to another base I divide repeatedly by the target base and read the remainders from bottom to top.
175 divided by 16 is 10 remainder 15, so that's A and F, 0xAF.
For binary I'd divide by 2 repeatedly, or more quickly, write 175 as 128 plus 32 plus 8 plus 4 plus 2 plus 1, which is 1010 1111.
The shortcut between binary, hex and octal is grouping. Hex is four bits per digit, so I group the binary into nibbles from the right: 1010 is A, 1111 is F.
Octal is three bits per digit, so I group by three from the right: 10 101 111 is 2, 5, 7, so 0o257. So 175 decimal is 0xAF, binary 10101111, octal 257.
I'd check by converting back: 2 times 64 plus 5 times 8 plus 7 is 128, 168, 175. Good.
Two things I always watch: pad the leftmost group with zeros, and don't mix up the group direction, it always starts from the binary point."
